This happened years back, but reddit didn't exist then, let alone Voat, so it's going up now, I was at a sailing event with a large fleet of small boats. Small, but large enough to anchor offshore and take small inflatables ashore to the barbeque or whatever was happening. I'm in the inflatable maneuvering through all the moored boats. At one point I have to shift into reverse, at the same time I slip and accidentally shift into full throttle.

I'll just say at this point that outboard motors aren't like cars, they don't have a complex gear box, they go forward and back at the same ratio with all speed being controlled by the throttle, so full throttle reverse means the engine is going as fast as it can backwards.

I barely had seconds to fix what I'd done, so I reached for the gear shift and tried to flick it into neutral, but I couldn't budge it, it was stuck. By this point the engine and my weight at the back of the dinghy were ploughing the stern down into the water. The inevitable happened and before I could reach up to throttle back, water flooded over the stern, and the whole boat did that slapstick thing where someone runs too fast on slippery ground and flips heels over head.

Amazingly my lifejacket inflated (they often don't) but I'm able to swim and I was conscious so it didn't matter all that much. The engine kept going for a second before it drowned (if you want to murder an engine quick, pour saltwater into the carburetter) and I was left swimming in a rapidly expanding pool of escaping petrol from the tank. Another boat came over to help and we tried to flip it back over. Normally this would be pretty easy, but we had been towing the boat earlier that day in rough weather and were worried about it flipping, so we lashed an anchor down low in the bows. When I flipped the dinghy the anchor broke loose and anchored it in place, upside down.

I'd imagine all this must have been very entertaining for all the people eating and watching on shore, a few of them bought me drinks afterwards which was nice of them. My shame eventually ended when we righted the boat and recovered all the bits and pieces. Amazingly the engine recovered with some TLC, although I wouldn't like to chance doing that again. To this day I'm extremely cautious about outboards and am reluctant to use anything more powerful than the minimum I can get away with.
